paras: The threatened lynching of William Mason and Thomas DeMoss took place in Topeka, Kansas, on the night of October 19, 1903, when a crowd gathered at the city jail after the two Black men were arrested in the fatal shooting of Fred Tutcher, a liveryman. Sheriff A. T. Lucas had already moved the prisoners to Lawrence, and the crowd dispersed without violence. Wire reports described a lynching mob of 200 to 1,000, while the Topeka State Journal and the Black weekly Topeka Plaindealer called it a gathering of spectators.

On Sunday, October 18, Mason and DeMoss hired a horse and buggy at the Tutcher & Son livery barn and drove it back hard after 11 o'clock that night. When Tutcher reproved them, according to the witness P. L. Reed and Tutcher's dying statement, DeMoss raised a buggy whip and Mason shot Tutcher in the abdomen. The two men confessed but claimed self-defense, saying Tutcher came at them with a club, which Reed denied.

Police traced the pair through B. A. "Buck" Wilson, a third man seen with them that afternoon, and arrested both on October 19. Tutcher died that afternoon; a dispatch said the authorities expected an attempt on the prisoners "as many threats have been made." Lucas sent both men to the Lawrence jail before dark, on the six o'clock train according to the wire.

After dark a crowd gathered around the city jail. The State Journal counted three or four hundred spectators without leaders; the wire said about 200 "formed a mob," and that a committee from the crowd, invited by officers, searched the jail, found it empty, and the crowd dispersed. According to the local paper, groups of Black men openly carried shotguns, rifles and revolvers, and Police Chief Goff refused his officers' requests to disarm them, saying the whites were probably armed too. A Topeka dispatch printed in Marshalltown, Iowa, reported nearly 1,000 people at midnight "intent upon lynching," fifty armed Black men in an alley ready to fire on any leaders, and threats to follow the prisoners to Lawrence.

A coroner's jury found that Tutcher died from a bullet fired by Will Mason, and both men were charged with first-degree murder. At Mason's trial in December the defense planned to contest his confession as made in fear of a mob. On December 8 the jury took nineteen minutes to convict him of first-degree murder; he was sentenced to hang, but since no governor would set a date he went to the penitentiary for life on January 7, 1904. DeMoss pleaded guilty in March 1904 to third-degree manslaughter and received one to three years.

The first wire reports named DeMoss as the man who fired, and the threats dispatch ran under headlines such as "Negro Murderers Fear the Lynchers" in the Salt Lake Herald. Weeklies ran the follow-up as "Wanted to Lynch Them. Sheriff Lucas Outwits a Mob," and the Barton County Democrat headed it "Attempt to Lynch Two Negroes." The Marshalltown paper called the accused "two negro toughs."

The State Journal headlined the night "Danger of a Clash Between Blacks and Whites," placing the threat chiefly on armed Black men. Its October 24 editorial acknowledged local sentiment for lynching "the two miserable wretches" but welcomed its passing, arguing that meeting one murder with another would not bring the victim back.

The Plaindealer also condemned the killing, as "A Fiendish Act," but denied any danger of lynching, calling the crowd curiosity seekers drawn by reports of lynching talk "which was not true." It credited the sheriff, police chief and courts with making mobs unnecessary and did not mention the armed Black men described in the white papers. In November the Plaindealer and the Sedalia Times listed "Mobs after Negroes at Topeka" among recent outrages.

Crowd figures range from about 200 in the wire and 300 in a Dodge City special to nearly 1,000 in the Marshalltown dispatch, against three or four hundred spectators in the two Topeka papers. The State Journal had the whites gone by 11:30, which conflicts with the Iowa dispatch's midnight gathering. A September 1904 State Journal list of convictions swapped the two men's outcomes, contrary to its trial reports.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of William Mason and Thomas DeMoss
bases: A crowd gathered at the Topeka city jail with talk of lynching two Black prisoners accused of murder, who had already been removed to Lawrence; no one was harmed (A4, A5, A10).

No one was killed or injured: the prisoners were moved to Lawrence before the crowd of 200 to 1,000 gathered over the shooting of Tutcher, and it dispersed (A4, A8, A10); this was at most a threatened lynching.

Independent local and wire reports agree that a crowd gathered at the jail after the prisoners were moved (A4, A8, A10, A19), but the State Journal's news story and the Plaindealer deny that it was a mob or that lynching was a real danger (A4, A12).

accounts.label: Black editor (Topeka Plaindealer)
accounts.gist: The crowd was curiosity seekers drawn by newspaper talk of lynching, which was not true; local officers' record meant no mob was needed.

framing.detail: Kansas and Nebraska weeklies ran 'Wanted to Lynch Them. Sheriff Lucas Outwits a Mob'; the Barton County Democrat titled it 'A Mob at Topeka. Attempt to Lynch Two Negroes'.

The State Journal called the shooting 'A Fiendish Deed', denied the crowd was a mob, blamed armed Black men for the danger of a clash, and editorially opposed lynching while calling the accused 'miserable wretches'.
Out-of-state wires headlined the prisoners' fear: 'Murderer Fears Lynching', 'Negro Murderers Fear the Lynchers'; Marshalltown's 'Trouble at Topeka' called them 'negro toughs'.
The Plaindealer condemned the killing as 'A Fiendish Act', denied any lynching danger and praised local officers; later Black weeklies listed 'Mobs after Negroes at Topeka' among outrages.

versions.value: three or four hundred spectators, not a mob

conflicts.note: The two Topeka papers, local and written within days, agree on three or four hundred and deny it was a mob; the Iowa dispatch's 1,000 at midnight conflicts with the State Journal's report that the whites were gone by 11:30.
The State Journal itself later wrote of lynching sentiment (A17) and that 'a mob gathered' (A24).
The first-day reports named DeMoss; the confessions, coroner's jury and trial put the revolver in Mason's hand.
Wilson was the third man who identified the pair (A2); the Marshalltown dispatch appears to have confused him with Mason.
